## Learning question

> Which incentives preserve an unsafe or inequitable practice?

The first three lenses showed costs, harms, and hidden labor. This lens asks why they persist.

[Slides: CC BY 4.0. Lesson page and worksheet: maehr.github.io/stochastic-parrots-and-beyond]{.source}

::: notes
Ask: "Who decided which AI tool you can use at your institution?" Collect answers. Most decisions were made at a level above the researcher.
:::

## 1. Concentrated resources

- AI is made of models, data, labor, development frameworks, and computational power.
- A few companies control most of these resources.
- "Openness alone does not perturb the concentration of power in AI."

[Widder, Whittaker, and West (2024), Nature.]{.source}

::: notes
Point out that this is a material analysis: it starts from what AI is made of, not from what companies say about it.
:::

## 2. "Open" is a claim to check

- More than 45 generative AI systems, 14 dimensions of openness.
- Many "open" systems are "open weight" at best.
- Many providers withhold information on training and fine-tuning data.
- Openness is composite and comes in degrees.

[Liesenfeld and Dingemanse (2024), FAccT.]{.source}

::: notes
Ask: "What would you need to inspect, document, and cite a model in a publication?" Weights alone are rarely enough.
:::

## 3. Models encode the goals of their makers

- Every model simplifies the world according to the priorities of its makers (O'Neil 2016, ch. 1).
- A system optimized for engagement, market share, or a fast release can conflict with the goals of research.

## 4. Institutions set defaults

- Universities decide which tools to license, which to recommend, and which data may leave the institution.
- These defaults shape practice more than individual intentions.
- Procurement and policy are places of leverage, not only of compliance.

::: notes
This concept prepares Panarchy: the university is one of the levels.
:::

## 5. Regulation: the EU AI Act as one example {.smaller}

From 2 August 2025, providers of general-purpose AI models must, under Article 53:

- keep technical documentation,
- inform providers who build on the model,
- have a policy to comply with EU copyright law,
- publish "a sufficiently detailed summary about the content used for training".

Free and open-source models with public weights are exempt from the first two duties, unless they have systemic risk.

Fines are possible from 2 August 2026. Models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 have until 2 August 2027.

[Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, arts. 53, 101, 111(3), and 113. Not legal advice.]{.source}

::: notes
Do not answer whether the Act applies to a specific project. Note such questions for the legal service.
:::

## Case: an "open" license {.smaller}

[Documented case]{.label}

| Question                               | Llama 2 license (2023)                     | Open Source AI Definition 1.0 (2024) |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| Any purpose, without permission?       | No: 700 million user threshold, use policy | Required                             |
| Outputs may improve other models?      | Not other large language models            | No such restriction                  |
| Weights available?                     | Yes, under the license                     | Required                             |
| Detailed information on training data? | Not required                               | Required                             |

[Sources: Meta (2023); Open Source Initiative (2024); Maffulli (2023).]{.source}

::: notes
The OSI stated in July 2023 that the Llama 2 license is not open source. Ask: "Why does the word matter?" Reputation, and in the EU fewer regulatory duties.
:::

## Who gains, who pays?

![](../../assets/cases/04-stakeholder-map.svg){fig-alt="Map with the model provider in the center. Around it: cloud and hardware suppliers, data creators, data workers, universities as licensees, individual researchers, research participants, regulators, and the public. Arrows show money, data, and rules."}

[Original diagram. CC BY 4.0.]{.source}

::: notes
Read one arrow of each kind: money, data, rules. Ask which arrow is missing for the research participants.
:::

## Activity · 15 minutes

**Map stakeholders and incentives.** Groups of three or four, on paper or on a laptop.

1. Choose a research-use card from your group. Use Llama 2 only if no card fits. (3 min)
2. Place the stakeholders. For each: gains, costs or risks, leverage. (7 min)
3. Circle one incentive that keeps an unsafe or inequitable practice in place. (2 min)
4. Write one feasible governance change: who acts, at which level, by when. (3 min)

[Worksheet: Lens 4, stakeholder and incentive map]{.source}

::: notes
Collect the governance changes on the wall. They are the first material for Panarchy.
:::

## Expected output

A **stakeholder and incentive map** for each group:

- stakeholders with gains, costs, and leverage,
- one circled incentive,
- one feasible governance change with an actor, a level, and a date.

- [Regulation (EU) 2024/1689](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), the AI Act.

## Takeaway

> A practice persists when someone gains from it. Find the incentive, then find the level where it can change.
